analysis.one_liner: Bans housing discrimination against renters using vouchers, veterans, and military families.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the Senate Banking Committee and receiving one hearing in March 2024, it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Housing Act to make it illegal to refuse to sell or rent housing to someone because of where their money comes from — including housing vouchers, Social Security, disability benefits, child support, or help from family — as well as because they are a veteran or active-duty service member. It never got past the Senate Banking Committee: it received one hearing in March 2024 and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who rely on housing vouchers (Section 8), Social Security or disability benefits, child support, or help from family members, all of whom can legally be turned away today in many states because landlords refuse non-wage income. It would also protect veterans and active-duty service members, who the bill adds as protected classes, and would make it a federal crime to intimidate or interfere with someone exercising these new rights. About 2.3 million households use federal housing vouchers, so this is a protection aimed squarely at low- and moderate-income renters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders, veterans, and low-income renters

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income,' 'veteran status,' and 'military status' as protected classes throughout the Fair Housing Act, covering the sale and rental of housing, brokerage services, and lending. The bill explicitly defines 'source of income' to include Section 8 vouchers, federal, state, and local rental assistance, Social Security and disability benefits, railroad retirement benefits, child support and spousal support, payments from trusts or relatives, and savings.

Makes it a federal crime under the Civil Rights Act of 1968's fair housing enforcement provision to intimidate or interfere with someone because of their source of income, veteran status, or military status — the same enforcement tool used for race and religion.

Preserves the ability of organizations to continue providing services and assistance specifically to people receiving housing assistance, so landlords and nonprofits offering extra help to voucher holders would not be penalized for doing so.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and rental property owners, who could no longer screen out tenants simply because they pay with a voucher, disability benefits, or child support. Some small landlords would face higher administrative costs to process voucher paperwork and comply with fair housing enforcement. The federal government would bear modest costs for enforcement and for the bill's transition period for state and local fair housing agencies.

drawbacks.text: The bill places real compliance burdens on landlords, especially small ones: they would have to handle voucher program paperwork and follow federal fair housing complaint procedures, and a landlord who runs afoul of the new rules faces federal litigation risk. Landlord groups have historically argued that voucher payment rates set below market rents make renting to voucher holders a losing proposition for small property owners.

The bill changes who landlords must consider but does not change how much vouchers pay or provide any new funding, so it addresses discrimination without addressing the underlying shortage of affordable units or the gap between voucher values and market rents.

The bill gives state and local fair housing agencies a 40-month window (extendable by 6 months) to become federally certified to enforce the updated law, meaning full protections could take years to reach every state.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it protects — voucher holders, veterans, retirees and disability recipients, and families receiving child support — the benefit is direct: a legal right to be judged on ability to pay rather than the source of the payment, backed by federal enforcement. The cost falls on landlords, primarily in paperwork and the loss of the ability to screen out voucher tenants, and the bill does nothing about voucher funding levels or housing supply, which limit how much difference the protection makes in practice. It is a genuine anti-discrimination measure with a real but narrow reach; its main failure is not its design but that it never came to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee for the rest of the Congress — it got one hearing in March 2024, but the committee never voted to send it to the floor, and the Senate never voted on it.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Kaine introduced the bill on April 25, 2023 with 12 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
A total of 15 senators cosponsored the bill — 14 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents. No Republican cosponsored it.

The Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill on March 12, 2024 (printed as S.Hrg. 118-548), but the committee never reported the bill out and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners who can still turn away voucher holders and tenants living on benefits or child support are better off, since the federal protection never arrived. Senators who preferred to leave source-of-income rules to the states also got the outcome they wanted without having to vote against a fair housing bill on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords; senators who avoided a vote

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 4 independents cosponsored, and none of the 49 Senate Republicans did, so the bill never had a path past committee.

industries.note: The bill would end the common practice of refusing tenants who pay with Section 8 vouchers, disability benefits, or child support, forcing landlords to compete for those tenants on the merits. Small landlords in particular would take on voucher program paperwork and compliance costs.

industries.industry: Real estate brokers and mortgage lenders
industries.note: Sections 805 and 806 of the Fair Housing Act, which the bill amends, cover brokerage services and real estate transactions, so agents and lenders could not refuse services based on source of income, veteran status, or military status.

industries.industry: State and local fair housing agencies
industries.note: The bill keeps these agencies as the certified enforcers of fair housing law and gives existing agencies a 40-month transition window to meet updated certification requirements, locking in their role rather than creating a new federal enforcement body.
